script: Today I will walk through how we implemented a physics-informed model for bonded thickness in PDMS dip coating, what the first tests show, and what we plan to do next. The practical goal is to predict bonded thickness while incorporating physical restrictions we already know. We are evaluating two separate questions: whether a prediction respects those restrictions, and whether it is accurate on measurements the model has not seen. The numerical results come from runs archived through October 11. The data-preparation status reflects our October 14 update: values needed for every proposed loss term are available, but some datasets still need aggregation and preprocessing.
transition: First, I will explain what a physics-informed neural network is without assuming an ML background.

script: Think of a neural network as an adjustable mathematical relationship between measured inputs and an output. Its parameters are numerical coefficients, rather than separately identified physical constants. Training means repeatedly adjusting those coefficients so predictions agree better with examples. A physics-informed neural network, or PINN, also uses physical knowledge to guide the relationship. Following the diagram, inputs enter the network, the network predicts bonded thickness, and we score agreement with measurements and selected physical rules. Those scores guide the next parameter update. A loss is simply the numerical error score that training tries to reduce. Classical PINNs often use governing differential equations. Our current model uses a thickness bound and smoothness penalties; it does not solve an established governing adsorption equation. The diagram illustrates the training idea, while the later architecture slide shows the actual network size.
ifAsked: A rule can enter as a hard restriction that every output must satisfy, or as a soft penalty that discourages undesirable behavior. Our thickness bound is hard. The derivative penalties are soft.
transition: With that framework, here is what we have implemented and what the initial evidence says.

script: We now have a compact network, comparison models, and a record of each experiment. The comparison models tell us whether the added physics actually helps, rather than assuming a more sophisticated model must be better. On measured data, the PINN's root mean squared error is about 0.122 nanometers, while gradient boosting reaches about 0.065 nanometers on the same held-out rows. Lower error is better. On the synthetic test, the PINN reaches about 0.056 nanometers, but random forest still performs better. These are different datasets and test distributions, so the lower synthetic error is not evidence that experimental performance improved. The strongest established property is the thickness bound. The current tests do not yet establish an accuracy benefit from the added penalties.
ifAsked: A baseline is a reference model. An ablation removes or changes one component so we can investigate what that component contributes.
transition: The implementation developed in several stages, which this next slide summarizes.

script: Version 0.1 established a measured-data baseline with three inputs, a bounded neural network, and a smoothness penalty. We then evaluated it against simpler alternatives and checked behavior at concentrations beyond the training range. Version 0.2 added the larger synthetic study with seven inputs, an exploratory concentration-monotonicity test, and support for the remaining physics terms. Monotonicity means testing whether the prediction should consistently increase or decrease as a chosen input changes. We also added a dated run register and saved the exact code, configurations, and results. The versions identify implementation changes; they do not imply that every new version is more accurate. The remaining loss inputs are available, and the next integration step is to aggregate and preprocess their datasets.
transition: Before discussing the model itself, I will distinguish the measured and synthetic data used in these tests.

script: The measured baseline contains 58 observations and 16 concentration levels. That is a small dataset for estimating a flexible relationship. The synthetic source contains 3,000 rows, which are generated examples rather than 3,000 new laboratory measurements. We screened the source for invalid numerical or physical values. Some rows have nonpositive concentration or total thickness, and some have bonded thickness greater than total thickness. A row can fail more than one check, so the exclusion counts overlap. We excluded 192 unique rows and retained 2,808. This screening makes the data consistent with our input and output requirements; it does not establish experimental independence or validate the synthetic generator. We also preserve original row identities so exclusions remain traceable.
ifAsked: Synthetic data can help test optimization and represented relationships, but performance on synthetic examples needs separate confirmation on independent measurements.
transition: The next slide shows exactly which quantities each archived model received as inputs.

script: A feature is an input quantity given to the model. The measured run used concentration, uncoated-layer thickness, and total thickness. The synthetic run added four solvent descriptors. This table describes the prepared tables used in the reported runs, rather than the full set of values now available across our datasets. Bonded thickness is the quantity we predict, so it is never supplied as an input. We take the natural logarithm of concentration to compress its wide numerical range. We then standardize inputs by subtracting their training-set mean and dividing by their training-set standard deviation. This puts different quantities on comparable numerical scales without claiming they have the same physical effect. Only training data determine those transformations. Because measured total thickness is an input, this is conditional inference from film state, rather than prediction from recipe settings alone.
ifAsked: Preprocessing includes matching samples, harmonizing units, checking values, and applying transformations. We must confirm the recorded concentration units before giving the fitted relationship a mechanistic interpretation.
transition: Here is how those inputs pass through the network and how we enforce the physical bound.

script: The implemented network has two internal layers, with 16 units in each. A unit forms an adjustable combination of its inputs and applies a smooth nonlinear function. Tanh, or hyperbolic tangent, is the smooth function used inside these layers. We chose it because the loss calculation needs second derivatives. In the equation, z represents the standardized inputs, theta represents the adjustable parameters, and f is the network's raw output. The sigmoid function maps that raw output into a fraction between zero and one. Multiplying the fraction by measured total thickness gives predicted bonded thickness. The hat means predicted, B means bonded, and T means total. This construction guarantees a nonnegative prediction no larger than a valid positive total. The model has 353 adjustable parameters with three inputs and 417 with seven inputs.
ifAsked: The guarantee concerns the allowed range of the prediction. A value can satisfy that range and still be far from the actual bonded thickness. These fitted parameters are not independently identified adsorption constants.
transition: The output transformation supplies the bound. The following loss terms guide how the model learns within that bound.

script: The loss combines an error score for each selected objective. The data term penalizes disagreement with measured bonded thickness. The curvature term discourages a highly wavy fitted response. Lambda denotes a coefficient that controls the importance of a penalty relative to data fit. In the reported default PINN runs, the data coefficient is one and the curvature coefficient is 0.001. The separate concentration experiment uses a monotonicity coefficient of 0.01. Velocity curvature and the hydrodynamic residual have zero coefficients in the reported runs, so they do not influence those fits. We have the values required for all of these terms. The remaining datasets still need aggregation and preprocessing before we activate them. A zero coefficient describes what we used in those runs; it does not mean the physical values are unavailable.
ifAsked: The thickness bound has no coefficient here because the architecture enforces it directly. A weighted penalty can trade off against other errors; a hard output restriction cannot be violated by that tradeoff.
transition: The next slide gives the mathematical definitions, but the main idea is the behavior each term discourages.

script: There is no need to read every summation aloud. Each summation averages an error over a set of training rows. The first expression squares the difference between predicted and measured bonded thickness, after scaling by the training target's standard deviation. In the other expressions, q is the scaled prediction and z is a standardized input. A first derivative is the local slope of the prediction as an input changes. A second derivative describes how quickly that slope changes, or curvature. The smoothness term penalizes curvature across input directions. The monotonicity term penalizes slopes with the opposite sign to a selected hypothesis. The velocity term applies curvature penalization specifically to the velocity input. Here, n counts data rows, m counts rows used for derivatives, and d counts input features.
ifAsked: J is the selected set of monotonic inputs, and s chooses the expected direction for each. These are local, soft penalties. The derivatives are taken in standardized coordinates, so their magnitudes are not raw physical-unit derivatives. Automatic differentiation computes them from the model's mathematical operations, rather than estimating them from noisy neighboring measurements.
transition: These terms connect to the four physical constraints originally proposed for the project.

script: This slide separates the proposed constraints from what actually influenced the reported fits. The thickness bound is active by construction. General input curvature is also active in the default PINN loss, although it is not a direct test of withdrawal-velocity smoothness. We separately tested a positive concentration-monotonicity penalty. Velocity curvature and hydrodynamic scaling are implemented, and their required values are available, but their datasets still need aggregation and preprocessing. We should therefore describe them as awaiting data preparation. For the other monotonic relationships, we also need to inspect the prepared data and assess whether a consistent direction is justified. Having a value available does not automatically establish the physical hypothesis. No result shown later should be interpreted as including the currently inactive terms.
transition: The hydrodynamic term is a useful example of both the physics and the preparation needed before activation.

script: LLD refers to Landau-Levich-Derjaguin dip-coating scaling. The capillary number compares viscous effects with surface-tension effects. It combines viscosity, withdrawal velocity, and surface tension. The next expression estimates wet coating thickness for the applicable flat-plate, Newtonian regime. We apply a separately supplied wet-to-dry factor before comparing that estimate with predicted dry mobile thickness. The predicted mobile thickness is total thickness minus predicted bonded thickness. That distinction matters: this residual constrains the mobile layer and does not establish a governing law for bonded adsorption. The needed values are available. We must aggregate matching samples, harmonize units, and preprocess the datasets before using the term. We also check the applicability flag, conversion factor, and capillary-number gate for each eligible row.
ifAsked: A residual is the mismatch between a model prediction and a physical relation. Only eligible rows enter this residual. The wet-to-dry factor must be independent of the bonded target, so we do not build the answer into the constraint. The small-capillary-number threshold is an initial gate, not a guarantee that every other assumption holds.
transition: With the architecture and loss defined, here is how the parameters were fitted and how we made the comparisons fair.

script: Adam is the numerical optimizer that adjusts network parameters using the slope of the loss. The learning rate controls the size of those adjustments. An epoch is one training iteration over the full training set in this implementation. We allow up to 1,500 epochs and stop early if validation error does not improve for 150 epochs. Gradient clipping limits unusually large updates, and weight decay discourages unnecessarily large parameter values. A fixed seed controls random initialization and sampling so a run can be reproduced, but one seed does not establish robustness. The bounded network comparison uses the same bound without the physics penalties. The standard network uses the same internal layers with an unrestricted output. Random forest averages many decision trees, while gradient boosting builds a sequence of trees that correct earlier errors.
ifAsked: A decision tree makes predictions through a sequence of input-based branching rules. Matching data splits and keeping the test out of model selection is more important than making these different model families look architecturally identical.
transition: The next slide explains what training, validation, and test mean in these experiments.

script: Training rows determine the adjustable model parameters. Validation rows help select a checkpoint, meaning a saved set of parameters from a particular training stage. Test rows provide the final held-out comparison and do not select the checkpoint. We grouped rows by concentration, so an entire concentration level stays in one partition instead of being spread across training and test. This is a harder and more relevant check than randomly separating nearly identical examples. The high-concentration test asks whether the model can predict beyond the range represented in training. The measured and synthetic studies have different sample counts and distributions, so comparisons should be made within each shared split. Synthetic parent identities remain unresolved, so concentration grouping alone does not prove that the underlying source experiments are independent.
ifAsked: Data leakage means information that should be reserved for evaluation influences training or selection. Fitting preprocessing only on training rows prevents one common form, but it cannot by itself resolve unknown synthetic ancestry.
transition: Now we can interpret the first measured-data benchmark.

script: Every model here predicts the same 18 held-out measured rows. The bars show root mean squared error, or RMSE, in nanometers. It squares each prediction error, averages those squares, and takes the square root, so larger misses receive extra emphasis. Lower bars are better. The PINN is about 0.1223 nanometers, while gradient boosting is about 0.0649 nanometers. The bounded network without the curvature penalty is almost identical to the PINN, so this test does not establish an accuracy benefit from the default penalty. MAE is mean absolute error, the average magnitude of a miss. R-squared compares squared error with predicting the held-out set's own mean. A negative value means worse squared error than that reference. Zero observed bound violations is a separate result from predictive accuracy.
ifAsked: The tree models also had no observed violations on these test rows, but only the bounded architecture guarantees the range for any valid total. A single small holdout is exploratory evidence, not a stable estimate across independent batches.
transition: The next test shows particularly clearly why satisfying the bound does not ensure accurate extrapolation.

script: The horizontal axis is recorded concentration and the vertical axis is bonded thickness. The symbols compare actual measurements with PINN and random-forest predictions at concentrations reserved for testing. Extrapolation means predicting beyond the training range, where the fitted relationship has less direct support. At the high end, the PINN predictions rise well above the observed bonded thickness. Its RMSE is about 0.617 nanometers, compared with about 0.0294 for random forest. The PINN still remains below total thickness, so the bound works even though the prediction is inaccurate. All models have negative R-squared here. The observed bonded values span a very narrow range, so that metric has a small reference variance and can become extremely negative. We should read it alongside error in nanometers and the actual points.
ifAsked: The increasing measured total-thickness envelope may contribute when the predicted fraction extrapolates poorly, but we have not established that as the cause. A monotonicity or physics prior must be tested rather than assumed to fix this failure.
transition: The larger synthetic study answers a different question: how the model fits the represented generated distribution.

script: This benchmark uses the 2,808 retained synthetic rows, seven inputs, and 442 shared held-out rows. The PINN's RMSE is about 0.0557 nanometers and its R-squared is about 0.905. This indicates a reasonably close fit within this synthetic test distribution. Random forest still has the lowest error, about 0.0359 nanometers. The bounded and standard neural networks are also slightly better than the default PINN on this split, so we still do not have evidence that the curvature term improves accuracy. These results cannot be compared directly with the measured benchmark as an experimental improvement. The data source, feature count, and distribution all changed. Zero observed bound violations again describes these test rows, while the architecture provides the explicit global range restriction for valid totals.
transition: The parity plots make the individual prediction errors easier to see.

script: Each point represents one of the same 442 held-out synthetic rows. Observed bonded thickness is on the horizontal axis and predicted bonded thickness is on the vertical axis. A perfect prediction lies on the diagonal. Points above the line are overpredictions, and points below it are underpredictions. Both panels use matching axes, so we can compare the scatter fairly. The random-forest predictions lie closer to the diagonal overall, consistent with its lower RMSE. The PINN shows a wider spread, especially in parts of the lower and middle range. Overlapping points may hide repeated or very similar synthetic examples. Their density should not be interpreted as an equal number of independent laboratory observations.
ifAsked: These plots show prediction agreement, not calibrated uncertainty. The spread of points does not give a confidence interval for a new experimental sample.
transition: We then changed one loss setting to investigate the concentration-monotonicity hypothesis.

script: An ablation is a controlled comparison in which we change one component while holding the rest fixed. Here we added a penalty against negative concentration slopes. A partial derivative asks how the model changes with concentration while the other model inputs are held fixed. The fraction of training rows with a negative local concentration slope fell from about 43.44 percent to 40.99 percent. That is a modest reduction, rather than a guarantee of monotonic behavior everywhere. Held-out RMSE became slightly worse, from about 0.055718 to 0.056009 nanometers. The bars break the training-gradient diagnostic into viscosity-associated groups. These correlated synthetic solvent groups do not isolate a causal viscosity effect. This experiment therefore tests a hypothesis and does not justify adopting the penalty as the default.
ifAsked: The slope percentages are training-set diagnostics; they were not estimated by tuning to the test set. A soft local penalty can leave violations and can trade off against data fit.
transition: The learning curves show another part of the initial testing: how the fitting process evolved over time.

script: The horizontal axis counts epochs, or repeated full-training-set optimization steps. The vertical axis shows the base-ten logarithm of normalized mean squared error. The logarithm lets us see large early errors and smaller later errors on the same plot. A vertical value of zero corresponds to normalized error one, and minus one corresponds to 0.1, so a decrease of one unit means a tenfold reduction. The blue line is training error and the gold line is validation error on rows not used for parameter updates. In the measured run, validation selected epoch 76 and patience stopped training at 226. In the synthetic run, the selected checkpoint was the final allowed epoch, 1,500. That motivates a validation-based study of the optimization budget; it does not promise better test performance from longer training.
ifAsked: Different runs normalize by different training target scales, so these plots describe optimization within each run rather than comparing absolute nanometer accuracy across datasets. A training-validation gap can suggest overfitting, but the plot alone does not establish a single cause.
transition: These diagnostics also guide which architecture changes are worth trying next.

script: An architecture specifies how the model's mathematical operations are connected. Our initial choice is a compact multilayer perceptron, or MLP, which maps a short list of numerical inputs to a scalar prediction. Tanh makes it smooth enough for the derivative penalties. More elaborate choices address specific problems. A modified or gated MLP can help when different loss terms produce competing training gradients. Fourier features add sinusoidal representations that can describe variation at different scales, but could also fit noise without sufficient evidence. A Bayesian PINN represents uncertainty in fitted quantities, which still requires checking that uncertainty against measurements. DeepONet and Fourier Neural Operator learn mappings between functions or fields. Our present table contains scalar inputs and outputs, so those operator models are not the immediate next step.
ifAsked: The literature motivates candidate methods; it does not establish an adsorption law for this material system. We should choose added complexity in response to a demonstrated failure and evaluate it on the same protected test structure.
transition: To make those comparisons meaningful, each experiment needs a clear record.

script: Each row identifies a distinct archived experiment, including the implementation version and its PINN result. The newer runs record execution times prospectively. The older runs did not record those times, so they remain unknown instead of being reconstructed from file modification dates. Reproducibility also needs more than a timestamp. We preserve the exact settings, source snapshot, data identity, partition membership, predictions, and selected checkpoint. A checkpoint is the saved set of learned network parameters. A hash is a compact digital fingerprint that changes if the underlying bytes change. The integrity checks confirm consistency of the saved artifacts with the published versions. They help us reproduce and audit the experiment; they do not prove the physical hypothesis or scientific conclusion.
transition: Putting the results together, here is what we can and cannot conclude at this stage.

script: The bounded output construction guarantees a physically allowed thickness range for valid total-thickness inputs. That is a useful property, but it is different from predictive accuracy. On the current measured holdout, the tree baselines outperform the PINN. On the synthetic holdout, the PINN fits the represented distribution, but random forest remains stronger. The current model also uses measured film-state information, including total thickness, so it is not yet a recipe-only predictor. Independent experimental batches and synthetic parent identities still matter for evaluating generalization, meaning performance on genuinely new cases. We have not established calibrated uncertainty, a governing adsorption equation, or a causal mechanism. Finally, the additional loss values are available, but those datasets still need aggregation and preprocessing before we can report their effect.
transition: The next steps focus first on preparing those available data, then on testing whether each additional loss improves measured-data predictions.

script: Our immediate priority is to aggregate the available datasets and make the quantities consistent across matched samples. That means aligning sample identities, confirming units, checking values and timing, and producing model-ready tables. We can then preprocess the available physics inputs, verify the applicability conditions, and enable the remaining loss terms one at a time. That controlled sequence lets us identify which term contributes to a change. We should also repeat random seeds and use grouped cross-validation, which rotates independent groups through held-out roles to assess stability. New independent experiments should remain reserved as a final test. If we study synthetic augmentation, we must split the measured parents before generating training examples. The decision criterion is improved performance on protected measured tests, rather than only a lower training loss or a better synthetic score.
ifAsked: Available measurements do not remove the need for preprocessing or applicability checks. The current holdout results are already exploratory, so repeated model decisions should ultimately be assessed on fresh independent data.
transition: The final slide lists the methodological references and the repository containing the evidence behind this update.

script: These papers provide background for physics-informed learning, hard constraints, training difficulties, and possible alternative architectures. They are methodological references, rather than evidence that a particular bonded-thickness mechanism applies here. The repository contains the implementation, design decisions, data audit, experiment register, and archived numerical outputs used in the figures. The results shown are through October 11, with the October 14 clarification that all proposed loss values are available and the remaining datasets need aggregation and preprocessing. For discussion, the main near-term decision is how to combine and validate those datasets before comparing the additional losses on consistent splits.
